title: English Language & Literature MYP 5 eAssessment-style Practice Paper 2

questions.content:
Text A (a travel-writing extract, written for this paper)

The road to Qala Huma does not so much climb as lose its temper. For three hours the minibus coughed upward through switchbacks, its driver humming over a radio that offered only static, until, somewhere above the cloud, the engine gave a final shudder and stopped. 'Altitude,' he said cheerfully, as though naming a distant cousin.

I stepped out into a silence so large it seemed to have weight. Below us the valley had vanished under a white quilt of mist; above, the peaks were pink and sharp as broken glass in the early light. The air tasted of cold stone and woodsmoke. A woman in a bowler hat and a shawl the colour of beetroot appeared from nowhere, pressing a cup of something steaming into my hands. I did not ask what it was. It was sweet, and bitter, and it tasted like being forgiven.

By the time the engine restarted, I had been adopted: a grandmother had inspected my boots, a small boy had offered me a potato, and a dog had chosen my left foot as a pillow. I had come looking for a view. It was embarrassing how quickly I stopped looking at it.

Read Text A and answer the questions.

(a) Identify two details from the first paragraph that suggest the journey to Qala Huma was difficult. (2 marks)

(b) Explain what the final paragraph suggests about how the narrator feels about the village. (2 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
(a)
[1] One relevant detail, e.g. the road 'lose[s] its temper'; the minibus 'coughed' upward; the radio gave only static; the engine 'gave a final shudder and stopped'.
[1] A second, different relevant detail from the first paragraph.
(b)
[1] A valid inference, e.g. the narrator feels welcomed, happy and accepted by the villagers.
[1] Supported by a reference or quotation, e.g. 'I had been adopted'; the grandmother, the boy and the dog show kindness; 'It was embarrassing how quickly I stopped looking at it' shows the people mattered more than the view.
Accept other valid inferences supported by the text.

Text A (a travel-writing extract, written for this paper)

The air tasted of cold stone and woodsmoke. A woman in a bowler hat and a shawl the colour of beetroot appeared from nowhere, pressing a cup of something steaming into my hands. I did not ask what it was. It was sweet, and bitter, and it tasted like being forgiven.

By the time the engine restarted, I had been adopted: a grandmother had inspected my boots, a small boy had offered me a potato, and a dog had chosen my left foot as a pillow. I had come looking for a view. It was embarrassing how quickly I stopped looking at it.

Analyse how the writer uses language and structure in Text A to present both the harshness of the landscape and the warmth of the people. (6 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
[1] Identifies and explains the personification 'lose its temper' (or 'coughed'), which makes the road and vehicle seem alive and difficult, with a humorous tone.
[1] Comments on the sensory description of the landscape, e.g. 'a silence so large it seemed to have weight' or 'sharp as broken glass', creating an impression of vastness and danger as well as beauty.
[1] Comments on the contrast between the cold, harsh setting ('cold stone') and the warm details ('woodsmoke', 'steaming'), showing human warmth within a hostile landscape.
[1] Analyses the simile 'it tasted like being forgiven' or the contrasting pair 'sweet, and bitter', suggesting comfort and relief after hardship.
[1] Comments on structure, e.g. the movement from the difficult journey to the stillness of arrival to the quick succession of the villagers' kindnesses, which shows the narrator being drawn in.
[1] Analyses the ending, e.g. the short, wry final sentence and the list of three actions ('inspected', 'offered', 'chosen') showing the people have replaced the view as the focus; uses accurate terminology and supports points with quotations.
Accept other valid analysis supported by the text.

questions.content:
Text B (a short script for the stage, written for this paper)

THE LAST REHEARSAL

Setting: a school hall, early evening. Chairs are stacked against the walls. MARA, sixteen, stands alone on the stage holding a script. MR ODELL, the caretaker, enters pushing a mop bucket.

MR ODELL: (jangling his keys) Half six, Mara. I lock up at half six.
MARA: (not looking up) Just five more minutes.
MR ODELL: You said that at six.
(Pause. The mop bucket squeaks. MARA lowers the script.)
MARA: I keep forgetting the same line. Every time. It's the only line that matters.
MR ODELL: (leaning on the mop) Which one?
MARA: 'I was never afraid of the dark; I was afraid of being left in it.' (She laughs, shakily.) See? It's fine when it's just me.
MR ODELL: Then say it to me.
MARA: You're the caretaker.
MR ODELL: Thirty years I've swept this floor. I've heard every line in this hall, most of them wrong. (He sits on a stacked chair.) Go on.
(MARA straightens. The lights hum. She opens her mouth, then closes it.)
MARA: (quietly) I can't.
MR ODELL: (standing, picking up his keys) Tell you what. I'll count to ten. Slowly.
(He turns his back and begins to mop. The squeak of the mop is the only sound. MARA takes a breath.)

Explain how the writer uses stage directions and the structure of the scene to build tension and show the developing relationship between Mara and Mr Odell. (6 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
[1] Comments on the opening stage directions and setting (empty hall, stacked chairs, evening), which suggest isolation and a sense of time running out.
[1] Explains how Mr Odell's repeated reference to locking up at half six creates a ticking-clock pressure.
[1] Comments on the use of sound in the directions, e.g. the squeaking bucket, the humming lights and the silence, to emphasise Mara's hesitation.
[1] Explains how stage directions about Mr Odell, e.g. 'leaning on the mop', 'He sits', reveal him changing from impatient to patient and supportive.
[1] Comments on structure, e.g. the build-up to the key line, Mara's failure to say it ('I can't') and the unresolved ending, which creates suspense.
[1] Analyses Mr Odell turning his back to count, which shows empathy by removing the pressure of an audience; uses accurate terminology and supports points with quotations.
Accept other valid analysis supported by the text.

(a) Identify the writer's main purpose in Text B and the audience it is most likely written for. Give evidence for each. (2 marks)

(b) Explain how the writer uses language in the dialogue to show a difference in how Mara and Mr Odell speak. (2 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
(a)
[1] Purpose: to entertain and to explore an emotional struggle (stage fright, fear of being unheard), supported by evidence such as the line 'I was never afraid of the dark; I was afraid of being left in it'.
[1] Audience: a theatre audience or school and young-adult readers who can relate to performance anxiety, supported by evidence such as the school hall setting and teenage lead.
(b)
[1] Mr Odell uses short, direct, informal sentences and a practical tone, e.g. 'Half six, Mara' or 'Tell you what'.
[1] Mara's language is more hesitant and emotional, e.g. the broken sentences 'Every time. It's the only line that matters', or the fragment 'I can't'.
Accept other valid points supported by the text.

questions.content:
Text C (a poem, written for this paper)

TIDE TABLE

The sea keeps a diary in salt,
a page each day on the sand,
and each day the water forgets
what it wrote, and writes again.

My father read it like a timetable:
low at six, high at noon, the gulls
reliable as clerks. 'Be patient,'
he would say. 'It always comes back.'

Now I walk the long edge alone,
boots filling, pockets heavy with shells
I cannot name, and the page is blank,
and the water is learning me by heart.

Analyse how the poet uses language, imagery and structure in Text C to present memory and loss. (6 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
[1] Identifies the extended metaphor of the sea keeping a 'diary in salt' and explains how it suggests memory, record and impermanence.
[1] Explains the effect of the repetition and cycle in 'forgets ... writes again', which suggests nature's endless renewal in contrast with human loss.
[1] Comments on the simile 'like a timetable' and 'reliable as clerks', showing the father's calm, orderly view of the world.
[1] Analyses the father's direct speech 'It always comes back', and its irony or poignancy when the speaker is now alone.
[1] Comments on structure, e.g. the movement in time from the sea in general, to the past, to the present ('Now'), mirroring the speaker's loss.
[1] Analyses the closing image 'the water is learning me by heart', which reverses the earlier ideas of reading and forgetting and may suggest the sea now holds the memory; uses accurate terminology and supports points with quotations.
Accept other valid analysis supported by the text.

Text C (a poem, written for this paper)

TIDE TABLE

The sea keeps a diary in salt,
a page each day on the sand,
and each day the water forgets
what it wrote, and writes again.

My father read it like a timetable:

Compare how Text A and Text C present the writers' relationship with a place. Refer to both texts in your answer. (6 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
[1] Identifies a similarity, e.g. both use personification or natural imagery to make the landscape seem alive (the road that 'lose[s] its temper'; the sea that 'keeps a diary').
[1] Identifies a difference in tone: Text A is humorous and light, whereas Text C is reflective and sad.
[1] Compares the relationships with other people: in Text A strangers welcome the narrator, whereas in Text C the speaker is alone and remembers a father.
[1] Compares form and structure: Text A is prose with a narrative sequence from journey to arrival, whereas Text C is a short free-verse poem in three stanzas moving from general to past to present.
[1] Compares endings: Text A ends with joy and a sense of belonging, whereas Text C ends in uncertainty or a blank page.
[1] Supports the comparison with an accurate quotation from each text and reaches a supported overall judgement about how each writer presents place.
Accept other valid comparisons supported by the texts.

questions.content:
Write a piece of descriptive writing of about 400 words called 'Arrival'. You may write it as a travel-writing extract or as the opening of a short story. Use a place you know or have imagined. You should aim to engage a teenage reader.

You will be assessed on your purpose and audience awareness, the structure of your writing, your descriptive techniques and the accuracy and variety of your language. (12 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
[1] The purpose, to describe and engage, is clear and sustained.
[1] There is clear awareness of a teenage audience, with an appropriate tone and content.
[1] The chosen form (travel writing or story opening) is recognisable and the register is consistent.
[1] The opening is engaging and establishes the place or situation quickly.
[1] A clear and logical structure takes the reader through the arrival, e.g. a shift in time, focus or mood.
[1] Ideas are developed with specific, well-chosen detail rather than general statements.
[1] Sensory description is used effectively (sight, sound, smell, touch, taste).
[1] A range of devices such as simile, metaphor, personification or contrast is used purposefully.
[1] A distinct voice or atmosphere is created and maintained.
[1] Paragraphs are used effectively and linked with suitable connectives or references.
[1] Vocabulary and sentence structures are varied, including sentence length for effect, and spelling, punctuation and grammar are mostly accurate.
[1] The ending is effective, e.g. a closing image or reflection that links back to the opening.
Credit any valid approach that meets these qualities.
